We present a timing model designed to assess algorithm performance within HOL, a first-order logic based proof assistant. First, we develop a simple timed language supporting stateless definitions accompanied by a sound operational semantics provided as a HOL definition. Subsequently, we extend this framework to handle definitions that exhibit state and those forming cycles, ensuring soundness remains verified throughout. This flexible model serves to establish performance bounds for recursive algorithms often found in library programs, with all proofs regarding the correctness of this extended framework remaining machine checked within HOL.

Accurately predicting the turbulence characteristics at boundary layers is essential to understanding the physics of the near-wall flow. Nevertheless, challenges in modeling the instantaneous turbulent structures at these boundaries have persisted despite numerous two-equation turbulence models utilizing near-wall information. This study introduces data-driven techniques aimed at refining the accuracy of the coherent framework-based models for boundary turbulence prediction. Performance enhancements are achieved by employing artificial neural networks (ANNs) established through regression on extensive experimental datasets. This data-driven sub-model utilizes instantaneous near-wall shear-stress fluctuations and Reynolds-stress anisotropies to forecast turbulent structures. Performance comparisons reveal significant improvements made by data-driven techniques, evidenced nearly twofold reductions in prediction errors. This study further demonstrates that incorporating spatiotemporal dependencies through long short-term memory (LSTM) networks enhances model capabilities. Finally, data-driven turbulence models utilizing experimental data demonstrate the potential for high-precision forecasting, achieving approximately 90% accuracy in this complex domain.

At strong magnetic flux, the Hofstadter spectrum reveals an $\mathrm{SU(2)} \times \mathrm{SU(2)}$ multiplet composed of Kramers pairs, signifying that the system conserves time-reversal symmetry but lacks particle-hole symmetry, which permits the manipulation of topological properties through an explicit mass term. Plasmonic and dielectric optical antennas have been independently developed to address specific limitations, yet no prior work has effectively hybridized them. Although dielectric antennas offer superior unidirectional radiation, they suffer from relatively lower light extraction efficiency (LET) compared to plasmonic ones. By combining the strengths of plasmonic and dielectric structures, our research introduces a hybrid nanoantenna capable of LET levels exceeding 50%. This is achieved through a metal-insulator-metal (MIM) antenna coupled to a surrounding dielectric hemispherical shell. Our findings demonstrate that this configuration significantly outperforms standard plasmonic dipole antennas while maintaining high LET and achieving previously unattainable operational wavelengths in the near-infrared spectrum. Additionally, unlike recent ultra-slim and ultra-narrowband dielectric dipole alternatives, this hybrid design remains compact, exhibits broad spectral bandwidth, and supports high-power optical emission.

This paper introduces a novel shielding mechanism that explains the friction between granular materials and metallic surfaces through both experimental tests and numerical modeling. Utilizing this mechanism, the study investigates the friction dynamics of a single spherical particle resting on a surface inclined at varying angles. By integrating results from these simulations with a theoretical framework, the work validates the new shielding mechanism. Furthermore, it outlines a computational method to measure the shielding force and examines how this mechanism is influenced by particle velocity and normal force.

We investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of silicene within a hexagonal boron nitride substrate influenced by a single row of surface-mounted manganese atoms. Utilizing first-principles calculations, we identify two stable configurations for the Mn adornment. Under these conditions, the system exhibits magnetic moments ranging from 4.88 to 5.71 Bohr magnetons per unit cell. Furthermore, electronic analysis reveals broad metallic behavior transitioning into parabolic semiconduct characteristics within the valence band region. These findings offer valuable insights for the design of spintronic and transport devices.

The limitation of unbalanced data is a significant challenge within the field of multi-category text classification. Although various methods have been proposed to mitigate class imbalance, the impact of Artificial Neural Network (GAN) based oversampling remains largely unknown compared to other strategies. The primary objective of this work is to develop a systematic framework for benchmarking different artificial oversampling strategies across the standard datasets, including AgNews, Reddit, Amazon reviews, and Twitter news. The proposed system evaluates several approaches, ranging from Random Over-Sampling (RS) and class-weighted training models to domain-specific strategies like W2R (a reader-focused strategy) and AGN (a non-reader strategy). The research demonstrates that while RS alone is generally ineffective, combining strategies can be highly effective, with the combination of W2R and AGN achieving the best results.

This study examines the interconnectedness between COVID-19 coverage and regional news consumption, along as the relationships among cases, deaths, and public interest at a granular level. Utilizing regional market data from Nielsen together with a news crawling and analysis framework established earlier, we observe distinct patterns: (1) media attention correlates positively with both the number of cases and deaths; (2) higher infection and death counts drive an increase in news consumption, yet this effect diminishes as numbers rise, indicating a trend toward habituation; and (3) as the region of focus transitions from the national scope to local jurisdictions, both the intensity of media stories and audience engagement decrease. Additionally, we assess interactions between news exposure and consumer behavior, confirming that elevated media coverage amplifies the impact of the pandemic on digital and offline spending.

This approach involves integrating the field on small overlapping patches arranged on a grid covering the calculation sphere, in contrast to other existing methodologies that rely on grid-based sampling on the sphere or far-field observations. We examine how the polarization of an ultimate proton in elastic scattering events $e\vec{p} \rightarrow e\vec{p}$ is transmitted from the initial state proton via radiative electron–photon and subsequent Compton interactions. Utilizing a semi-emporetical framework that combines quantum electrodynamics with the polarization asymmetry of proton photopion dissociation, we calculate this effect at intermediate energy scales. We find that even under experimental conditions characterized by "loose" constraints regarding the final-state electron detection angle, significant levels of electron-induced polarization transfer to the ultimate proton are feasible.

To maximize efficiency when training specialized models on small datasets, it is vital to create high-quality augmented data. This study presents a method to automatically generate augmented images by leveraging scene reconstruction via explicit neural radiance fields, followed by arbitrary viewpoint syntheses using ray sampling and volume rendering. Our reconstruction process jointly optimizes neural implicit surfaces, light sources, and rendering parameters, with fine-tuning performed via explicit affine transformations. Experiments demonstrate that the generated images closely mirror real ones and support diverse augmentation tasks. Ultimately, our augmented datasets drive superior performance in datasets such as CUB-200 and Food-101, proving especially effective in low-data regimes.

Spin masers represent the pinnacle of coherent microwave radiation achieved via spin ensemble amplification; however, their development has stalled due to challenges in creating a digital interface. This work introduces a spin-maser interface engineered for quantum digital operations, employing radiofrequency pulses to manipulate the alkaline maser by addressing both individual and collective states of the atomic electrons. Using a rubidium maser, the authors demonstrate the manipulation of single photons and ensembles spanning up to ten particles via optical methods, while simultaneously achieving resonant rubidion amplification at levels exceeding 17 decibels. These outcomes validate the feasibility of using optical systems for controlling devices that emit microwave amplifiers over ten decibels, thereby facilitating the interconnectivity of major machines operating within different frequency spectrums.

Dark energy and dark matter are often considered distinct entities, yet the possibility that they are the same remains a viable alternative in light of the cosmological constant's limited lifetime as dark energy. Neutralinos, the leading candidates for warm dark matter within the WIMP framework, could theoretically undergo radiative decay into two photons. We propose that neutralinos have dominated dark matter throughout cosmic history, resulting in their gradual transformation into a self-interacting form of dark energy. Consequently, the universe experienced a shift from neutralino-dominated to dark-energy-driven expansion. The accumulated gamma radiation spectrum from these decay processes offers a potential observational method to identify dark matter candidates and track their decay, potentially identifying them as the "leftovers" of original dark energy. Using this gamma spectrum, we can determine the transition epoch when the nature of dark energy shifted, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of dark energy's properties. Furthermore, the neutralino mass derived from the current acceleration age of the universe aligns well with predictions derived from the relic density in the early universe.

This work extends the polentime algorithm by Bodlaender et al., which exactly determines genus for forests, to a broader class of thick graphs. We introduce a randomized Newton method designed for distributed optimization tasks, specifically targeting the solution of large-scale convex problems with linear constraints. Our primary contribution involves a novel randomized Newtonial approach suitable for efficient execution within distributed environments. We demonstrate that this method achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ convergence rate for feasible points and an $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ rate for optimal values when $k$ denotes the communication rounds. Additionally, we detail a specialized gradient projection technique that leverages problem structure to reduce per-communication costs per node. Our algorithm is applicable to various scenarios, including those involving the convexity of functions derived from log-determinant forms and exponential forms, and it accommodates both smooth and non-smooth indicator function representations for linearly constrained convex optimizations. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques in terms of convergence speed and computational efficiency.

Transfer learning serves as a potent method for training neural networks, enabling the training of a target task by utilizing weights initially learned by a different task. While numerous studies have demonstrated its efficacy in Western languages like English, its application within non-Western tongues remains under-explored. This paper investigates transfer learning for identifying Hindi and Bengali hate-speech by utilizing Word2Vec embeddings pretrained on individual languages and on a combined dataset. We further assess the performance of neural networks when the source task involves textual classification of English hate-speech. We have engineered a gas Time Projection Chamber capable of detecting recoil nuclei from pro and heavier particles with high-resolution 3D positions by utilizing an "electrostatic lens" formed at the drift space adjacent to the detector plane. We have evaluated the chamber's performance by analyzing recoil events from two distinct reactions: proton recoil resulting from a mono-energetic 2.5 MeV gamma-ray source, and nuclear recoil arising from a natural samarium source. These evaluations include a quantitative assessment of ionization measurables, such as the specific energy loss at the drift readout plane ($dW/dd$) and the electron drift velocity. This study proposes these gas-based parameters as effective observables for assessing gas ionization quality and interpreting experimental data. We anticipate that such an efficient, highly precise system, capable of identifying both atomic electrons and nuclei in real time, will serve as a highly effective detector for applications ranging from dark matter searches to nuclear waste analysis.

In public health, the term "standard of care" denotes the accepted, most effective, and typically most expensive level of treatment required for a specific condition. Similar to machine learning models used for disease prediction which depend on the quality of training data, the standard of practice within clinical settings directly influences the performance accuracy of algorithmic tools, creating a feedback loop where algorithmic bias can emerge. For example, the algorithmic evaluation of driving behavior is used by automated vehicles to decide whether to intervene in risky maneuvers. Because this system is trained on historical logs of both driving and monitoring, the resulting algorithm replicates the inconsistent and costly nature of human-led moderation found in standard practices. Our study demonstrates that these intelligent algorithms for vehicle safety perform more equitably when they bypass human bias by adopting context-aware choice logic. Our proposed solution involves a method that utilizes context-specific rules to moderate automated algorithmic decisions, effectively mitigating biases rooted in inconsistent human supervision.

This work details the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, an initiative that evaluates unsupervised approaches for automatically recognizing entities from natural language text without relying on pre-defined lists of known entities. The goal is to assess methods for deducing the length, boundaries, and correct classification of entity mentions solely from text. The authors have provided text-based examples for over 400,000 entities drawn from Wikipedia, covering diverse categories such as chemical compounds, city names, and sports teams. The dataset is evaluated using standard extraction metrics including precision, recall, and the F1 score. The authors have also established baselines using five unsupervised approaches, such as using training data to train a conditional random field (CRF) model or a lexicon-less approach using a conditional random field (CRF) model to achieve a baseline performance level. Among these measurements, some prove sensitive to higher-twist Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs), thereby enabling a novel approach to extract CIGPs without relying solely on unpolarized or beam-spin asymmetries which remain sensitive only to two real amplitudes out of twenty available combinations specifically using these methods. The study suggests that integrating these unique polarization-based observables will significantly broaden the JEFF dataset acquired at JEFF to fully explore seven essential DVFS parameters while providing critical access to various types of CIgPs previously unavailable. The study emphasizes how incorporating these novel measurements enhances our understanding of nucleon quark-gluonic dynamics by enabling precise extraction of both real and imaginary components in CIDp amplitudes while offering unprecedented insights into various types of CIgPs.

Our cognitive abilities to conceptualize objects and understand their interactions serve as a differentiator between humans and machines, motivating the goal of endowing Artificial Intelligence (AI) with similar object comprehension skills. Currently, AI systems lack a unified understanding of what constitutes an object. This work proposes a novel "Object Comprehension" framework for AI that aligns closely with human biology. Specifically, it draws inspiration from human vision research: where humans perceive both the visual appearance of an object and its properties (such as geometry and texture) to distinguish it—it shares this dual-processing mechanism with current AI, which typically separates object recognition from geometry/texture analysis. We argue these tasks should be integrated, advocating for an AI capable of perceiving geometric and textural nuances consistently with human biology. To achieve this, we develop an "Object General Knowledge" (OGK) structure that synthesizes deep learning-based recognition with rule-based reasoning, thereby enabling more effective AI interactions with the environment. Furthermore, incorporating human-like biases into these systems may boost performance; for instance, utilizing general knowledge of friction and gravity allows for enhanced accuracy in task planning. Additionally, our approach facilitates innovative algorithms for artificial creativity, such as generating games or musical compositions.

Through a combination of analytical and numerical approaches, this study examines the impact of spin-orbit coupling on superfluid stability within a lattice containing time or spatial periodicity. Our results indicate that as increasing the depth of this periodicity increases, both the critical temperature and critical flux rise, whether or not spin-orbit coupling is present. Notably, when a critical flux is surpassed, the supersolid phase remains intact, but a segment of the mini-Band Fermi surface converts to a gapped state. Furthermore, periodic deepening amplifies the magnitude of this induced spin-orbit coupling, thereby generating an additional gap within the fermi sea and modifying the thermal phase diagram.

We propose a novel regularizer for neural network optimization that promotes sparseness in the activations of hidden layers. This approach is conceptually rooted in Optimal Transport (OT) theory, which interprets the distribution of activations as a continuous process. By incorporating a global "speed limit" on how quickly activity can spread across the network, we create a barrier against sparse vs. dense distribution shifts, thereby encouraging overall sparsity. Because this objective lacks an analytical closed form, we derive an approximate solution using a specific variational inequality that can serve as its proximal surrogate. During empirical evaluation on a Convolutional Neural Network tasked with object classification within ImageNet, we demonstrate how varying the regularizer's strength systematically alters the proportion of zero values in the activations. Furthermore, we show that these sparse configurations do not compromise model accuracy, while also noting their potential benefits for downstream tasks such as object localization via region proposal generation in Convolutional Networks.

This study presents insights into the dynamics of a weakly interacting Bose gas subjected to strong confinement within the plane of strong spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that beyond establishing stable spin-momentum locked helical vortex states, such a system fosters Pauli-like blocking of excitations regarding spin winding modes when confined to two dimensions. Such behavior holds promise for investigating topological bosonic fluids and their associated bosonic analogues within quantum magnetism. Furthermore, our results suggest that quantum simulations on quantum platforms could offer pathways to realize topological phases characteristic of fermionic systems.

These days, implementing testing tools and frameworks has become more accessible and less costly. Despite this, software remains highly error-prone, prone to costly failures that necessitate testing to detect faults and ensure quality. While various testing techniques have been suggested to enhance the quality assurance process, they all demand a thorough understanding of the problem. Our previous research has identified and described "smells" in testing practices, outlining how they manifest and their detrimental effects. In the present work, we investigate the severity of testing odors from a developer's perspective through surveys. We analyzed responses to determine which smells are most severe for developers and examined how this perception shifts depending on the individual's experience level. Our findings reveal that these oars are indeed perceived as serious by developers, with individuals with less experience perceiving them as even more critical than those with extensive background knowledge.

Utilizing the Golec-Biernin and Koenig Cross (GBK) methodology for CCMMLet2 event generation, we examine several strategies for precise QCD radiation modeling, specifically analyzing how these choices impact the transverse momentum (P(T)) spectrum of the generated particles. Accurately determining the Inter-Beats (IBs) represents a significant challenge in music analysis, particularly for traditions like Hindustani music, where Ib intervals fluctuate irregularly. This paper presents the application of the Tiramisu deep learning framework to extract these intervals from audio signals. Our proposed model incorporates multi-scale attention mechanisms designed to evaluate the significance of various input lengths. Additionally, we address the inherent class imbalance in the data by implementing a weighted loss function. This study also details the creation of an original, structured dataset of Hindustani music. Evaluations using both an openly available music library and a proprietary database built from our new dataset indicate that the Tiramisu framework achieves superior IB assessment accuracy.

This paper introduces an algorithm for computing Tensor Singular Value Decomposition (TSVD) via T-SVD. The method is based upon a new class of stochastic algorithms called the Stochastic Algorithm for Matrix Singular Value Decomposition (SAA-SVD), which iterates to find extreme eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the core tensor. A key characteristic of our approach is its ability to handle a variable iteration count. This flexibility is advantageous when determining how many cycles to run, as it can be adjusted based on computational time budgets or required accuracy thresholds. The methodology integrates the Power Method into the core TSVD process, thereby accelerating the traditional T-SVD. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on two applications: hyperspectral imagery denoising and classification, with numerical results demonstrating its efficiency. Additionally, our approach significantly reduces computational costs compared to the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM).

Embedding dynamic graphs into low-dimensional continuous spaces is essential for analyzing time-evolving network structures. We integrated this metric with standard node embedding techniques to create a new algorithm capable of generating embedding vectors that reflect structural similarity across different temporal layers. Experimental results indicate that this approach enhances node classification performance, demonstrating that a multi-temporal, bottom-up training strategy outperforms traditional single-time-step training.

This study investigates a single static 2D monocular photograph taken by an eyepoint-in-hand camera mounted on an industrial robot arm to deduce the robot's camera extrinsic parameters relative to the end effector. Since intrinsic camera parameters are typically pre-calibrated, this study focuses specifically on learning the relative extrinsic parameters using a deep learning approach leveraged by computer vision. The novel approach presented in this paper utilizes a deep learning model to automatically extract 3D object structure from the 2D image, bypassing the conventional requirement for physical calibration targets like checkerboards. Using this approach, the paper demonstrates how to train a learning-based regression system to map the single 2D image directly into 6 degrees of freedom relative pose data. Theoretically, the study proves that a single 2D static image contains sufficient degrees of freedom to estimate the relative pose, provided that the 3D locations for at least four non-degenerate points are known. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that employing the known internal parameters significantly enhances the accuracy of the estimated relative pose data derived from such images.

We introduce a novel model-based reinforcement learning algorithm inspired by the concept that intelligent agents typically operate within specific operational domains. This model, known as "domain consistency," acts as an inductive regularizer to constrain the agent's policy to a reduced subset of the state space, thereby enhancing learning efficiency and robustness, especially in environments with vast state sets or limited data. By employing a deterministic domain con straint combined with the soft argmax operation, we can integrate this limitation into the standard Reinforcement Learning framework, presenting the resulting "Domain-Constrained Policy Gradient" algorithm. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the implicit learning of a condensed state representation, effectively replicating the capabilities of standard representation learning techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that these domain-constraints not only boost sample efficiency and performance but also serve as a mechanism for enhancing policy robustness against distributional shifts.

This study introduces a supplementary supervised framework designed to enhance the capabilities of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). While PINNs integrate a small set of known deterministic physics-based partial differential equations (PDEs) with neural networks to address complex systems, their deterministic components are insufficient when stochastic behaviors or unexpected events—such as wild fires or seismic activity—are involved. Consequently, our proposed supplementary model operates as a data-driven, fully stochastic deep neural network trained via the supervised generalized unsatisfied-based-potential (GUSBP) method. This approach quantifies risk by mapping input spatial-temporal variables to output probabilities of specific determinations. By utilizing supplementary probabilistic models, researchers can gain a granular understanding of uncertainty within high-stakes domains characterized by extreme variability. Furthermore, our framework enables precise localization of prediction errors and assessment of existing PINNs' reliability in the face of unforeseen scenarios. We validate this methodology across three distinct use cases: wild fire propagation, earthquake modeling, and gusty wind field reconstruction.

A spatiotemporal air pollution dataset was constructed by integrating data from 2006 to 2013 gathered by 25 monitoring stations in Milan, augmented with satellite-based satellite retrievals. To capture atmospheric contamination levels holistically, the study utilized the empirical Gaussian kernel for satellite data and Gaussian random fields for spatiotemporal pollution trends. This hybrid approach was then applied to investigate associations between exposure levels and health outcomes, specifically hospital admissions for respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, as well as deaths related to pneumonia and pulmonary insufficiency. Given that air pollution is a highly complex matrix of gases and particulate matter interacting chemically and physically, introducing a new geostatistics and deep learning-based artificial intelligence (AI) methodology is proposed. This solution addresses the dual challenge of performing reliable risk assessments while maintaining high predictive accuracy. Results from the AI-enhanced geostatistical models demonstrated superior performance over traditional empirical methods, yielding higher correlation coefficients and lower root mean square errors. The refined exposure estimation successfully enhanced the significance of statistical associations, providing a more precise quantification of air pollution's adverse impacts on human health.

We introduce a tunneling spectroscopy method that uses a resistive electrode, which effectively filters out minor noise peaks while isolating the dominant Majorana mode. While the existence of Majorana modes is a critical prerequisite for building robust, noise-immune qubits, their confirmation has proven surprisingly difficult. Repeated spectral measurements, often argued as a verification tool, are not truly unique because spurious modes may exist alongside potential Majorana modes. Instead, we demonstrate the mode's verify lies in observing a sharp tunneling peak—significantly larger than others—that remains unchanged across multiple dissipation levels. Using a resistive electrode to tune dissipation allows researchers to scan a wide range of values efficiently and quickly, rather than waiting for equilibrium at individual resistance settings. Furthermore, by analyzing the peak structure across the entire dissipation spectrum, one can pinpoint an optimal operating point where minor fluctuations are suppressed and dissipation is minimal.

A primary challenge in deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) is their sensitivity to adversarial attacks, where subtle data contamination shifts model predictions. Our work demonstrates that adversarial re-labeling attacks can effectively target the inherent inductive biases of GNNs, resulting in prediction shifts without requiring changes to the underlying architecture. Specifically, we introduce a reinforcement learning agent tasked with identifying optimal labeling strategies for a chosen graph structure to manipulate model outputs. We also present methods to evaluate these attacks, offering data-driven guidance for defending against such threats.

Photometry significantly enhances astrometry, a fact currently underutilized in catalogue alignment techniques. This study investigates how integrating simple photometric data improves methodological approaches, specifically focusing on three strategies: refining astrometric matching through photometric cross-identification, increasing matching precision via a chi-squared (χ²) metric, and enhancing star selection quality. Tests comparing these methodology variations across various sky regions and star types indicate that photometric enhancements are most effective for bright stars with well-defined photometric signatures, such as those exhibiting a large number of matched counterparts (10 or more) and reaching maximum matching success rates of 95%. Conversely, methods least effective rely on less distinct photometric characteristics and a sparse set of matched counterparts (fewer than 10), where performance peaks at approximately 80%.

This work addresses a question by J. Stepr\u0145a by investigating a hypergraph analogue of the Tychonoff plank. We demonstrate that if a set $X$ is at most a power of $ \aleph_0 $ in cardinality and lies within a simple, weak, or weak hereditary $\binom{n+2}{n+1}$-hypergraph $H$ (for any fixed $n \in \mathbb{N}$), then the minimum size required to cover all $\binom{n+2}{n+1}$-subsets of $X$ using $\binom{n}{n}$-subsets is strictly less than the maximum degree of the hypergraph, $d_H(X)$, provided $H$ is defined only on $X$. In contrast, we present a $\binom{n+2}{n+1}$-hypergraph $H$ rooted on a countably infinite set where the required covering size is determined by a specific relationship to the maximum degree of the hypergraph, demonstrating the sharpness of the hypothesis. This finding is significant for understanding how the properties of hypergraphs influence Tychonoff plank analogues.

Ontologies serve as a standardized method for explicitly defining data concepts and their interconnections, enabling diverse forms of meaningful interpretation to address specific inquiries. As a consequence of growing diversity in application scenarios, these definitions are increasingly structured within formal ontologies. To facilitate discovery and the resolution of challenges involving concept relationships, visualizing ontologies has become a vital practice for enhancing human understanding and interaction. Nevertheless, creating innovative visualization techniques remains difficult due to the vast volume and structural intricacy found in comprehensive ontology systems. While prior studies have predominantly focused on enhancing or tweaking existing tools like YEditor by means of the tree-based graph view, this approach proves inadequate for non-hierarchical connections, which are often overlooked in traditional hierarchical views. To address this shortcoming, we present Ontoplot, a new framework specifically engineered to manage non-hierarchical data in extensive ontologies. Our solution offers an intuitive interface that provides immediate access to available navigation and interaction tools. Furthermore, we have evaluated the utility of our approach against current industry standards, yielding findings that highlight its superior performance in representing non-hierarchical concept relations.

This paper introduces a fresh navigation approach centered around two fundamental self-regulating principles inherent to personal assistants: a motivation-driven framework and a loop for active deduction used to set targets. Through these mechanisms, the proposed system enables seamless robot movement to fulfill specific user requests. Unlike methods relying on explicit map data, this approach utilizes a basic visual representation of obstacles, facilitating an efficient adaptation to dynamic, non-deterministic environments. We describe a theoretical framework concerning the influence of molecular flexibility on the Soret effect, employing specific binary binary non-isothermal hydrodynamic equations to analyze the center-of-mass motion and orientational dynamics of an "infinitely dilute" sample. This theory examines two distinct solute species, namely hard spheres and two-state soft spheres switching between extended and collapsed states. It demonstrates that molecular shape fluctuations, alongside soft mode transitions, can significantly amplify the Soret coefficient compared to responses observed in rigid spheres or single-state models. This theoretical model's validity is confirmed through its strong alignment with results derived from non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, in scenarios involving collapsed spheres, an alternative relaxation mechanism emerges, distinct from those in extended states; this is anticipated to leave a significant imprint on the structure factor's frequency domain behavior.

Comprehending and evaluating student compositions demands a nuanced grasp of both grammatical correctness and deeper semantic coherence, which is the focus of this study. While recent studies have applied various neural networks to analyze writing, the specific methods for leveraging such evaluations remain underexplored. Consequently, the initial phase of this research involved a comprehensive survey of grammar and context assessments, which led directly to the architectural design of a new transformer-based system. Named AgCoEval, the system utilizes a pre-trained transformer along with a newly developed model that specifically targets semantic cohesiveness. AgCoEval was tested on the revised English portion of the ROCStories dataset, where it achieved state-of-the-art performance in composition scoring. Specifically, the system reached an F1 score of 0.7255 and a Correlation coefficient of 0.8255. Additionally, the study includes a thorough analysis of the system's predictions to highlight its capabilities and limitations within automated composition evaluation metrics.

Domain-adapted pedestrian identification relies heavily on pseudo-labels derived from weakly supervised semi-supervised clustering techniques. However, clustering often generates false positives due to the presence of outliers derived from the background. Experimental evaluations on two major benchmarks, PEZRD and PRW datasets, indicate that this method reduces 68% of false positives in PRW and 61% on PEZE, resulting in significant improvements for pedestrian identification accuracy.

We propose an end-to-end neural network that transforms musical audio waveforms into corresponding monochrome image representations. Leveraging established image editing techniques, specifically style transfer and colorization, we introduce two musical transformations: "Color Style" and "Monochrome Color." Furthermore, we implement a neural architecture capable of reversing the initial image-music conversion, utilizing the resulting edited images to apply practical audio effects. Our methodology bridges the distinction between perceptual audio manipulation and traditional image processing, offering a new, accessible interface for effect processing within the domain of musical audio.

The kinematic chain is a hierarchical structure of physical links and joints that, when activated, generate a resulting effect. In sports, the movement of a throwing animal is a key example, where the final link—the release of an object like a ball or weapon—marks the instant of release. Despite the extensive research into human sports performance, our understanding of the performance effects arising from release inaccuracies remains limited. This study aims to model and examine how a shifted Point of Release (POR) affects the trajectory and accuracy of a ball in both overhand and underhand throws. Our findings indicate that while a shifted POR has a negligible effect on the flight path of underhand-thrown objects, it significantly alters trajectories in overhand throws. Furthermore, we observe that the sensitivity of the overhand throw to release location increases as ball weight goes up or thrower mass decreases. Consequently, our results emphasize the necessity of precise release timing and technique in the overthrowing of heavy objects to achieve accuracy

Although graph-based models have demonstrated superior performance in tasks involving neural machine interpretation and parsing, they are hindered by the high dimensionality of their search space. This dimensionality arises from both the high node degree caused by the numerous possible children a node may possess and the extensive node count derived from the full syntactic structure. This study reintroduces a sequential, pre-order tree decoder, adapting it for machine interpretation by leveraging syntactic priors to constrain the search area. We propose a single-node, post-order reconstruction strategy utilizing syntactic linkers that sequentially builds an initial pre-order representation before refining it into the genuine parse tree by incorporating syntactic features to resolve structural ambiguities. Our method eliminates the need for auxiliary constituent identification, operates within a single decoder framework, and significantly reduces the search dimension. Furthermore, we establish that our linkers function effectively as indicators, enabling the model to capture long-range syntactic dependencies. Our experiments confirm that this approach achieves state-of-the-art results in machine interpretation as well as reaching state-of-the-art-level outcomes on standard parsing benchmarks.

Accurate energy values for molecular binding distributions are essential for advancing our knowledge of interstellar chemistry and planetary atmospheres within the context of the astrochemical field. To address this need, we have developed the Binding Energy Assessment: a platform that serves as a central archive for experimentally derived and quantum chemically calculated binding energy distributions. By providing ready access to these data, we aim to facilitate comparative analyses that will significantly improve future binding energy estimations utilized across various scientific domains. Binding data can be submitted: https://bit.ly/BAcP-submission. Already hosted on this platform are four experimental studies covering binding energies for CO, N2, and N on a variety of solid surfaces.

Log-normal distributions are suitable for many real-world, stochastic multiplicative processes. In this paper, we introduce a log-normal stochastic model that is designed to align with observed data by adopting a lower limit that is derived directly from a large sample. Using this adaptive lower limit as a constraint, geometric mean, and weighting factor, we establish a simulation equation. This model demonstrates its utility by generating realistic, multiplicative stochastic sequences based on lithium ion battery cycle data. Furthermore, we compare the statistical properties of our simulation against both the original dataset and various independent log-normal distributions.

We propose an operational method to evaluate hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, focusing primarily on those reliant on random Clifford circuits. By linking algorithm performance to the specific property of having shallow states within the random ensemble—the class of hybrid algorithms hybridized Clifford circuits, where key operations are effectively traced out—the algorithm's average value can be expressed as a function. This function represents the disparity between two distinct representations of the original hybrid circuit as a random Clifford state, measured in the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Specifically, the hybrid algorithm is cast into a tensor network structure, utilizing random self-maps to partition Hilbert space into subspaces. Within these partitions, hybrid operations are effectively traced out, while random Clifford components are assembled into a new tensor network that acts as a reference against which the algorithm's output is measured. This framework offers precise analytical insights into hybrid algorithms rooted in random self-maps, enabling broad generalizations. As a specific case study, we derive an exact formula for qubit alternating operator quantum algorithms, allowing for asymptotic analysis. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of this approach in other domains, such as variational quantum eigensolvers, quantum machine learning, other types of random self-map algorithms, and variational algorithms generally speaking across the quantum computing field across different algorithm types.

Neural network architectures have become a popular and often successful tool for classifying emails as spam or ham. However, this paper introduces Sibyl variants applied to recurrent networks, designed to stop these networks from being exploited to bypass trained class decision boundaries. The approach involves integrating sibyl modifications with a recurrent network that has bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). Experimental evaluations utilizing the Enron email corpus demonstrated that these Sibyl-based architectures achieve high accuracy while offering robust resilience against adversarial perturbations.

This work presents a method for automatically learning a consistent depiction—ensuring that the same entities appear identical in synthesized images—for multiple view angles based on a limited set of examples. We frame this challenge as learning the composition, orientation, and placement of the target object from just a few reference images. Our approach utilizes linear deformations to maintain entity depiction consistency across views. Specifically, trained on a dataset, the method first extracts objects and determines their composition and orientation. It then employs deformation synthesis to generate images for various viewpoints that maintain depictive consistency with the training set. We validate our approach using the ADE200 dataset, which includes over 2000 object instances across more than 400 categories, each captured in four different orientations. Experimental results indicate our technique successfully generates novel orientations that align visually with the training examples. Furthermore, we release our code at https://github.com/rao1998/mull.

Resource constraints often hinder the deployment of Neural Machine Translation (MT) models within low-capacity environments, such as embedded systems. Addressing this, two primary techniques have emerged: quantization and distillation. Quantization reduces model computational demand by lowering weight precision, while distillation constructs a compact network capable of replicating the target model's performance. Despite their established roles, a critical comparison of their robustness within these low-resource contexts is lacking. Consequently, we evaluate a multilingual system spanning nine languages through progressive reduction in precision, contrasting these results against a model distilled to match performance at lower accuracy thresholds across multiple languages. Findings indicate that larger models are more susceptible to failing to meet performance benchmarks in low precision environments compared to their distilled counterparts, revealing a robustness advantage for distillation in low-resource settings despite it being outperformed in both accuracy and efficiency by larger architectures under normal conditions.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in biomedical image segmentation, particularly within the detection and analysis of lung diseases. Despite advances made using self-supervised or transfer learning strategies, these methods often demand large-scale, fully labeled datasets to reach state-of-the-art performance levels. This study focuses on reducing the reliance on annotated data in medical imaging by enhancing training data quality rather than quantity. Specifically, we evaluated two enhancement strategies applied to training images: (1) training with cropped regions extracted from the dataset and (2) ensembling three enhancement models to generate training images. We assessed these approaches across three pneumo-na segmentation tasks varying by training data size (full dataset, 75%, 50%) and validated them using an external test set. Results indicate cropped regions outperform both full-image training and ensemble-enhanced methods across all data conditions. Furthermore, these region-based techniques achieved new state-of-the-art scores on limited-data scenarios, with an AUC of 0.811 at the 50% subset level.

Current image description models have become highly effective, yet their outputs can remain unnecessarily verbose or verbose, which is often undesirable. In many practical applications, such as image search or description generation, concise summaries that utilize fewer tokens are preferred. This work investigates controlling the cardinality (length) of word counts in the multi-task training setting. The study evaluates several post-processing techniques designed to compress descriptions without compromising semantic content, as well as direct training approaches aimed at generating concise sentences, though both face limitations, yielding suboptimal dual outcomes for description quality and length. To address these issues, we propose controlling the descriptive cardinality through direct prompting during training that penalizes word redundancy. This approach integrates length constraints within the standard multi-task framework, bypassing the need for post-processing sentence compression. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that our method outperforms existing techniques across varying density levels by delivering superior concepts and length management.

Although deep learning breakthroughs have been achieved with numerous frameworks, constructing models from the ground up still demands significant effort. While this process is generally manageable using Apache Spark MLlib, it lacks the scalability and flexibility required for truly cutting-edge deep learning applications. To bridge this gap, we present MMLSpark—an extension of Spark MLlib designed specifically for scalable and flexible deep learning.

Voice recognition for natural language tasks has traditionally been built upon the paradigm of supervised learning, necessitating extensive parallel speech and semantic annotation from voice speakers and semantic annotators in large volumes to function. This study introduces the novel concept of zero-shot voice interpretation, which functions with no, or minimal, speech and semantic annotation pairs. The novel approach utilizes transfer learning from language models and transfer learning from voice analysis models. This study demonstrates the ability to generate answers for different domains and languages without any domain- and language-specific data. While domain expertise represents a significant asset in machine learning, its systematic incorporation into predictive models remains unresolved. Given the varying granularities of an expert's knowledge, a KPI-driven K-Levels taxonomy is introduced to guide its in-depth exploration. Subsequently, two primary integration strategies are defined and illustrated using concrete examples, each supported by specific blueprints guiding their deep integration process points. Finally, this demonstration leverages well-established techniques within a knowledge-centric kernel learning framework to highlight how well-known algorithms can be reinterpreted and integrated into learning algorithms through the lens of domain expertise.

As the global community faces the ongoing threat posed by the Coronavirus pandemic, there is an urgent need for advanced tools to combat its impact. Lesion localization and segmentation represent two critical components within Computer Aided Diagnosis (CAD) for identifying the virus. However, existing datasets are predominantly biased toward cases from specific geographic regions, notably China, impeding the creation of impartial CAD solutions that generalize worldwide. In response, we introduce a novel, weakly guided learning strategy aimed at developing robust models capable of generalizing across diverse datasets without requiring fully annotated training data. Utilizing patch-level annotations, we demonstrate lesion localization and segmentation through the inference of shared domain-specific knowledge from fully annotated source models. We validate this framework using the open-access COVID-CT-Dataset, which includes scans from multiple countries. Our experimental results indicate that our approach achieves superior F1-scores compared to other methods, attaining 72.2% on an external test set.

Although deep learning-based vertebrae recognition and labeling from medical data have been widely investigated, current approaches often omit corrections for misaligned vertebrae, which can be attributed to patient posture or scanner errors. These factors can significantly degrade recognition accuracy. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a verticae alignment strategy that employs 3D registration to correct spinal curvature in CT data, thereby simplifying the subsequent labeling process. Furthermore, we propose anatomically constrained enhancement (Anatomicaolabelling), an algorithm designed alongside this rectification to produce precise, boundary-aware segmentation masks for each vertebra. These images are then utilized to train a recognition model that distinguishes the anatomical type of each vertebrae level within the CT volume. Experimental evaluation indicates substantial improvements in alignment quality as well as enhanced segmentation and classification metrics. Consequently, our methodology substantially aids automated procedures in tasks such as spinal disease diagnosis and preoperative planning.

We investigate the dynamical stabilization of a highly excited electronic state within an atomic system when it is in an empty optical cavity, yielding results that closely mirror those for strong laser fields. This stabilization occurs because rapid unitary evolution induced by the weak vibrational spectrum of the cavity prevents irreversibility in the system's electron dynamics. Specifically, we analyze an initial state where the electron is confined to one electronic level and the system contains one photon. By treating this photon as the driving force for extreme strong-light-mattering regimes, we examine how the system evolves into a state with zero photons. In this limit, we demonstrate that within a certain energy window known as the dynamical stabilization region, the population of the excited state remains bounded over time despite initial excitation due to the rapid unitary dynamics preventing permanent energy transfer. Finally, we highlight that this phenomenon holds significance for the field of polaronics by illustrating how electron scattering by photons in the vacuum under strong coupling leads to unique, non-classical behaviors.

While electric actuator technology has allowed for significant progress in legged robot control and task execution, these conventional rigid units are often too bulky and heavy for deployment in tight or extrave environments. In contrast, this study presents a systematic strategy for harnessing the high specific power of high-energy-density storage devices within low-complexity actuation hardware to support sophisticated dynamies. Specifically, we employ high-powered elastic actuators alongside energy-based and dynamic control methods to endow a quadruped prototype with the capacity for complex maneuvers. Experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of this approach in facilitating advanced dynamies using a minimal count of rigid, high-power components. Ultimately, this research offers a scalable path for deploying advanced robot capabilities in settings demanding restricted actuation density.

Based on this method, the study investigates the divisibility dynamics of several open-quantum systems, specifically focusing: (1) the divisibility behavior of quantum Brownian motion.

Fashion travelers often seek to locate apparel items whose visual style matches a specific item of interest. We introduce a new method to enhance this process through Feature-Level Trait Manipulation (FPM). Unlike traditional approaches, FPM alters specific aesthetic attributes within a given image to create novel variations, enabling users to search for these modified outcomes directly. By integrating this adaptation step into image retrieval, the system expands the scope of potential matches and encourages exploration. Our implementation utilizes a GAN-enhanced adaptive network that operates in a semi-supervised framework, learning both constant and changeable traits simultaneously. Consequently, this allows users to perform image searches based on trait-specific modifications, achieving superior search accuracy over state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines the resolution of a broad category of linear ill-posed problems within the framework of Banach spaces. Inspired by the classical Tikhonov regularization method, the work first establishes a variational representation for the minimum norm solution, leveraging dual gradient ascent techniques to approach said solution variably. Subsequently, it scrutinizes divergent and non-divergent information-based gradient-based schemes, demonstrating how each ensures the convergence of computed gradients to the minimum-norm solution under specified criteria, culminating in the formulation of a specific condition that marks when iterates are quiescently stable regarding perturbations in input data.

Light field imaging offers a practical, cost-effective method for Depth Assessment, yet dependence on precise optical intrinsics can introduce measurement inaccuracies. We introduce an Occlusion-Responsive Loss (ORL) tailored to light field data to compute depths, eliminating reliance on fixed optical parameters. Unlike conventional approaches that optimize for individual pixels, our proposed framework jointly models all subapertures to produce high-quality initial depth maps, which are then refined by integrating constraints from both image structure and intensity. To resolve inconsistencies, we incorporate an algebraic structure for loss computation to resolve circular dependencies, thereby creating an closed-loop algorithm. Experimental results indicate that our system performs on par with, or superior to, state-of-the-art methods requiring less computational time.

The increasing popularity of wireless Wi-Fi in residential settings, particularly high-speed broadband adoption, has necessitated extending network coverage beyond single rooms. However, simple extensions often exacerbate channel congestion problems, which degrade overall performance significantly. This paper proposes a novel algorithm that leverages IEEE 802.11k/v protocols, which are standard in current IEEE 802.11 implementations, to proactively detect and mitigate channel congestion proactively. This method is entirely client-driven, meaning it operates independently of AP roles. Additionally, this approach is compatible across all widely used wireless driver implementations known today. The process utilizes IEEE 802.11k probe and information element requests sent to the Access Point to gather available network data and determine best channels for each connected client device based on current usage patterns. The method has been tested using both real-world experimental results and simulation environments, demonstrating that it significantly improves channel utilization efficiency compared to static configurations. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is an intuitive and effective solution for resolving issues caused by improper extenders being paired with primary access points in home WiFi deployments.
